steps.html:
Some sentences are hard not because the words are difficult but because twenty-four of them stand between the subject and its verb. This lesson is about getting through those, and about the endings that turn a noun into an adjective.

  • Find the main clause inside a long sentence
  • Read a layered account and take the facts from it
  • Build adjectives with -ive, -al, -able and -ing
  • Write one long sentence that a reader can follow

steps.title: Find the verb, then the subject, then everything else
steps.sub: Read this before the texts. You will use it on the very first sentence.
steps.html:
A long English sentence is not one long idea. It is a short main clause with material packed around it, and the material is almost always when, where, why, which or who.

The technique has three steps, in this order. First find the main verb. Then ask what is doing it. Only then go back for everything else.

Try it on this: When the roof of the San José mine collapsed in August 2010, trapping thirty-three men at a depth of seven hundred metres, the company that owned it announced that the chances of survival were poor.

The main verb is announced. What announced? The company. That is the whole main clause: the company announced that the chances were poor. Everything before it tells you when, and everything inside that owned it tells you which company.

The commonest mistake is reading more slowly. Speed is not the problem; order is. Reading the words in the order they appear is exactly what makes a layered sentence hard.

steps.title: Text A · Before the drill arrived
steps.html:
Written for this course, from the Encyclopaedia Britannica account of the 2010 Chile mine rescue and contemporary reporting.

The San José copper and gold mine, which lies in the Atacama Desert some forty-five kilometres north of Copiapó and which had killed eight workers between 1998 and 2010, was closed in July 2010 after a rock fall cost a miner his leg, was allowed to reopen on the twenty-eighth of that month once corrective measures had been reported — an economic decision as much as a technical one — and collapsed one week later — a sequence that is almost never mentioned in the accounts which made the rescue famous, and which is treated, in most of them, as historical background rather than as the most relevant thing on the page.

When the main ramp closed at two in the afternoon on 5 August, trapping thirty-three men at a depth of seven hundred metres and five kilometres from the entrance, the group made for the ventilation shafts, which existed precisely so that men could climb out of a blocked mine and which should therefore have settled the matter in an hour; but the ladders required by the safety code were not there, and the men, having found the one route the regulations promised them and having found it unusable, went back down to the refuge to wait.

For seventeen days nobody above ground knew whether they were alive, and survival in that period depended not on the drilling equipment, which was still being assembled, but on the men themselves, who rationed two days of emergency food across a fortnight and organised, without being asked to, the shifts and the sleeping arrangements that a psychologist would later describe as the reason the mental strain never became unmanageable. Several exploratory boreholes missed the chamber entirely, the mine’s own maps having proved less reliable than anyone expected; the eighth found it, and came back up with a note attached.

steps.title: Text B · Where the telling begins
steps.html:
Written for this course, from contemporary reporting on the rescue and its aftermath.

What followed was impressive by any objective measure: three separate drilling plans running at once, of which the one that broke through was a rig normally used for boring water holes rather than for reaching people; a medical team on site well before the shaft was finished; and, on 13 October, an operation lasting about twenty-two hours which brought every one of the thirty-three to the surface and which an estimated one billion people watched.

What followed was also, in the way it was told, extremely selective, because the account that reached that billion began on the day the drill arrived rather than in the decade when the warnings were ignored, and a story that begins in the right place is inspiring in a way that a story beginning in the wrong one never is. A congressional commission afterwards placed the blame on the mine’s owners and on the state body that was supposed to inspect them, which is a sentence that appeared in far fewer places than the pictures did.

The ending is less tidy than the broadcast. Many of the men were left with lasting physical and mental difficulties, several were unable to work, and the compensation they were awarded — upheld by Chile’s Supreme Court in 2023, at about forty-eight thousand dollars each for the thirty-one who took part in the case — arrived thirteen years after the collapse. It is an unfortunate fact about rescues that the part which is easy to film is also the part that ends, while the medical and economic consequences, which have no obvious final image, continue long after the cameras have been packed away.

For seventeen days nobody above ground knew whether they were alive, and survival in that period depended not on the drilling equipment, which was still being assembled, but on the men themselves, who rationed two days of emergency food across a fortnight and organised, without being asked to, the shifts and the sleeping arrangements that a psychologist would later describe as the reason the mental strain never became unmanageable. steps.html:
Two recycled areas that both appear in the texts.

-ive comes mostly from verbs ending in -t or -de: impress → impressive, select → selective, object → objective, decide → decisive.

-al comes from nouns: history → historical, medicine → medical, mind → mental, nation → national. -ic is similar and often interchangeable in origin but not in meaning: historic ≠ historical, economic ≠ economical, classic ≠ classical.

-able / -ible means 'can be done': rely → reliable, manage → manageable, believe → believable. Add un- to reverse it.

-ing and -ed both make adjectives from verbs, and they point in opposite directions: the story was inspiring (it did the inspiring) and I was inspired (it was done to me).

And the recycled point: in a long sentence, a reported clause is often the thing you are looking for. The company announced that the chances of survival were poor. The main verb is announced; everything after that is what was announced, and it is not the main clause.

steps.title: Two adjectives from one noun, two meanings
steps.html:
1. The noun is economy, and it gives two adjectives that are not interchangeable.
  2. Economic means 'to do with the economy': economic reasons, economic growth, an economic crisis.
  3. Economical means 'not wasteful': an economical car, an economical use of space.
  4. The same split happens elsewhere. Historic = important in history (a historic day). Historical = relating to the past (historical research). Classic = the best example of its type. Classical = of ancient Greece and Rome, or of a formal musical tradition.
  5. The test: if you mean about the subject, the longer form is usually right. If you mean a good example of it, the shorter one is.

steps.title: Write your account.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Build at least three long sentences with material between the subject and the verb — and make sure a reader could still find the main clause in each.
steps.html:
• Open with a long sentence: time clause, participle clause, then the main clause.
  • Use <i>For … days, during which …</i> for the second.
  • Use <i>What … was …</i> to put the important thing at the end.
  • Close with a short sentence, for contrast.

Useful language

  • When … , trapping / leaving / forcing … , the … announced that …
  • For … days, during which … , nobody knew whether …
  • What reached them first was …
  • The … that followed, which took … , was watched by …
  • …, none of which is the main point.
  • It was objective, reliable and still almost unreadable.
steps.modelHtml:
The flood on the Nura

When the river rose eleven metres in a single night in April, flooding four villages and cutting the road in two places, the regional administration announced that the situation was under control.

For three days, during which about nine hundred people slept in a school gymnasium and volunteers drove the only route still open, nobody could say how many houses had gone.

What arrived first was not the emergency service but a line of private cars, which local people had organised themselves through a messaging group set up that same night.

The account that eventually appeared in the national press, which described the response as impressive and well coordinated, mentioned none of this. It was objective, it was reliable, and it was about a different event entirely.
